did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah’s prophecy against Ammon begins by asking why Ammon has taken possession of Gad and settled in the cities of Israel—a charge connected with seizing Israel’s inheritance.

Did you know? Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, is described as becoming a “heap of ruins,” and its villages will be burned; it is later said that Israel will take possession of those who took possession of it.
Did you know? Despite the prophecy of destruction against Ammon, the chapter ends with a promise: “Afterward I will restore the fortunes of the Ammonites.”
Did you know? Edom is described in the chapter as being renowned for its wisdom, especially in Teman, yet the text declares that the counsel and wisdom of its people will perish.
Did you know? Edom’s security is attributed to its high dwelling places and rocky strongholds; however, its pride will not protect it, and it will be brought down from its lofty abode.
Did you know? Edom’s destruction is described as so severe that everyone who passes by will be astonished and whistle at its wounds—the explicit comparison is to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah.
Did you know? The prophecy against Damascus also mentions Hamath and Arpad: the three cities hear bad news, lose courage, and are overcome by fear and flight.
Did you know? The calamity against Damascus includes not only the downfall of its warriors, but also the setting fire to the city wall and the burning of the palaces of Ben-hadad.
Did you know? Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor are described as communities with tents, flocks, and camels; Nebuchadnezzar is commanded to attack them and plunder the people of the East.

Did you know? In the prophecy against Elam, the breaking of the bow symbolizes the breaking of its military power, while scattering the people to the four winds represents their dispersal in every direction.
